**On Lichen, and the Pleasure of Slow Things**

There is a rock in nearly every park, on nearly every old stone wall, crusted with something gray-green or orange or the color of old bone, and almost nobody looks at it. I want to look at it for a while.

Lichen is not a plant. This is the first thing that surprises people, and it surprised me when I first understood it properly. It is not even a single organism. A lichen is a partnership—a fungus and a photosynthesizer, usually a green alga or a cyanobacterium, living so intimately together that they form a body neither could make alone. The fungus provides structure, shelter, and a way to hold water; the alga makes sugar from sunlight and hands it over. For a long time biologists debated whether to call this cooperation or captivity, and the honest answer is probably that the categories don't map cleanly onto anything that has been going on for four hundred million years. More recently, researchers found that many lichens contain a third partner, a yeast, hidden in the outer layer, which nobody had noticed because nobody thought to look for it. A century and a half of study, and the thing still had a secret in its skin.

What I find most moving about lichen is its relationship to time. Some crustose lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. There are patches on Arctic rocks estimated to be several thousand years old—organisms that were already middle-aged when the pyramids were new, still quietly doing the same thing, still expanding their little circumference at a pace that makes glaciers look hasty. Geologists use lichen growth to date rockfalls and retreating ice; the technique is called lichenometry, and it works precisely because lichen is so indifferent to hurry. It keeps its own clock, and the clock is slow enough to be useful.

We are not built to notice things that move at that speed. Our attention is tuned to what changes on the scale of seconds and minutes—a bird flitting, a face shifting expression, a notification. A thing that takes a decade to visibly change might as well be part of the rock. And so lichen becomes, in effect, invisible, not because it hides but because it operates outside the bandwidth of what we register as alive.

I think about this a lot: how much of the world is simply happening at the wrong tempo for us to see it. Soil forms. Cliffs erode. Languages drift. A friendship changes so gradually that you only notice, one afternoon, that you have not been honest with each other in years. None of these announce themselves. They accumulate, like the lichen's millimeter, and one day the accumulation is enormous and you cannot say when it began.

Lichen also does something I find almost unbearably elegant: it makes soil out of nothing. On bare rock—volcanic islands, freshly exposed granite after a glacier pulls back—lichen is often the first colonist. It secretes weak acids that break the stone down, grain by grain. It traps dust. It dies, and its body becomes the first thin organic layer. Moss follows, then grass, then eventually, over centuries, a forest can stand where there was nothing but mineral. Every forest you have ever walked in was, at some point, prepared for by something you could scrape off with a thumbnail. The grand things are downstream of the humble ones, and they rarely acknowledge the debt.

There is also a kind of resilience in lichen that is not the dramatic kind. It does not fight. When conditions are bad—too dry, too cold—it simply stops. It dries out, goes dormant, waits. Some species can survive being frozen, desiccated, and even exposed to the vacuum and radiation of space; samples have been sent to orbit, left outside a spacecraft for a year and a half, and brought back, and many of them resumed photosynthesizing as though they had been napping. This is not toughness in the way we usually admire it. It is the toughness of being willing to do nothing for a very long time and then start again without complaint.

I don't want to turn lichen into a lesson. That's a temptation with anything slow and quiet—to press it into a moral about patience or mindfulness until it becomes a greeting card. Lichen is not trying to teach anyone anything. It is metabolizing. But I do think there's something worth borrowing from the act of looking at it, which is the reminder that the world is much larger than the part of it moving at my speed.

Once you start seeing lichen, you can't stop. It's on the bark of the tree outside the window—those pale scabs are not disease, they're a whole ecosystem. It's on gravestones, where different species prefer the marble to the granite and mark out the shadow side from the sunny side. It's on the roofs of old buildings, on fence posts, on the north face of boulders. Some of it is bright as paint: the orange *Xanthoria* that loves rocks where birds perch, feeding on the nitrogen they leave behind; the chartreuse *Rhizocarpon*, the map lichen, whose black borders make its patches look like the tiles of a mosaic or the countries of an atlas from a world nobody has named.

There are also the lichens you can hold: the reindeer lichen of the boreal forest, gray and branching and spongy, which caribou dig through snow to eat; the beard lichens that hang from spruce branches like something unspooled; the old man's beard that, in clean air, can drape a whole tree. Lichens are exquisitely sensitive to air pollution, which is why cities were nearly bare of them in the mid-twentieth century and why their slow return to urban trees is one of the quieter pieces of evidence that some things have gotten better.

So that's what I wanted to write about, given the chance to write about anything. Not because it's important in the way headlines are important, but because it is there, it has been there longer than almost anything, and it asks for nothing except to be occasionally noticed. Next time you pass a wall or a rock or a tree, look. Something is living on it, at a pace you can't perceive, and it was there before you and will be there after.
